questions.q: Which is NOT one of the seven essentials of a valid contract?
choices: Consideration
A registered title
Capacity
Genuine consent
questions.explain: The seven: offer, acceptance, consideration, legal intention, capacity, legal object and genuine consent.

questions.q: Under the Law and Equity Act s.59, what do contracts about land generally need to be enforceable?
choices: A seal
To be in writing
A lawyer's signature
Registration at the LTO
questions.explain: Land contracts generally need to be in writing to be enforced.

questions.q: A contract signed by a minor is best described as what?
choices: Void from the very start
Voidable at the minor's option
Valid and binding on both sides
Illegal and unenforceable by anyone
questions.explain: Under the Infants Act it's unenforceable against the minor but enforceable by them, so effectively voidable at their option.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Four ways a contract can fail

questions.q: An oral agreement to sell land that both sides intended to be binding is usually what?
choices: Void, as if it never existed at all
Unenforceable due to a procedural bar
Illegal, so courts refuse any relief
Voidable at either party's option
questions.explain: It may be a real agreement, but without writing it hits a procedural bar and is unenforceable.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Four ways a contract can fail

questions.q: A listing on MLS® with an asking price is legally what?
choices: An offer to sell to the first full-price buyer
An invitation to treat
A standing offer to the whole public
A binding option for buyers
questions.explain: Ads, listings and displays invite offers; they aren't offers themselves.

questions.q: A seller's counter-offer says "open until 9 p.m. Friday." Can the seller revoke it at 3 p.m. Thursday?
choices: No, a stated deadline makes it irrevocable
Yes, if it's revoked before acceptance
Only with the buyer's written consent to it
Only if the seller pays the buyer damages
questions.explain: An offer can be revoked any time before acceptance, despite an "open until" date, unless an option was paid for. Revocation must be communicated.

questions.q: When does revocation of an offer take effect?
choices: When the offeror decides to revoke
When the offeree actually learns of it
When it's mailed to the offeree
When the offer's deadline passes
questions.explain: Revocation must be communicated (Byrne v. Van Tienhoven). The postal rule doesn't apply to revocations.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · When does acceptance take effect?

questions.q: Which of these does NOT end an offer?
choices: A counter-offer made by the offeree
An inquiry about changing the terms
The offeree's outright rejection of it
The offeror's death before acceptance
questions.explain: A genuine inquiry doesn't kill the offer; a counter-offer or rejection does.

questions.q: A seller accidentally accepts two offers on the same property. What's the usual result?
choices: Both buyers must share the property equally
The first in time wins; the other gets damages
The higher of the two offers automatically wins
Both contracts are void for mutual mistake
questions.explain: The earlier contract gets the property; the seller is liable in damages to the other buyer.

questions.q: What makes an option agreement different from an ordinary "open until" offer?
choices: It must be registered at the Land Title Office
Separate consideration keeps the offer open
It can be revoked at any time before acceptance
It can only be used in residential transactions
questions.explain: Paying separate consideration makes the promise to hold the offer open binding. Options are common in land assembly.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Option agreements: keeping an offer open

questions.q: In Livingstone v. Evans, why could the buyer still accept after making a counter-offer?
choices: The counter-offer was never sent
The seller's reply renewed the original offer
Counter-offers never end the original
The court found the seller acted in bad faith
questions.explain: "Cannot reduce price" was read as renewing the original offer, which the buyer then accepted.

questions.q: Which statement about acceptance is correct?
choices: Silence can be acceptance if the offer says so
Acceptance must be a clear, positive act
Acceptance can add new conditions freely
Acceptance needn't be communicated
questions.explain: Silence isn't acceptance, and acceptance must match the offer. New terms make it a counter-offer.

questions.q: Under Rules s.47, what must a licensee do once an offer is accepted?
choices: File a copy of the contract with BCFSA
Promptly copy it to each party and the brokerage
Read the full contract aloud to both parties
Register the contract at the Land Title Office
questions.explain: Rules s.47: promptly deliver a copy of the accepted contract to each party and the brokerage.

questions.q: An acceptance is properly mailed Monday and arrives Thursday. When is the contract formed?
choices: Thursday, when it arrives
Monday, when it's posted
When the offeror reads it
Only when the offeror replies
questions.explain: Under the postal rule, a non-instantaneous acceptance takes effect when posted.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · When does acceptance take effect?

questions.q: When does an acceptance by phone take effect?
choices: When it's spoken
When it's received by the offeror
At midnight on that day
When later confirmed in writing
questions.explain: Instantaneous methods take effect on receipt by the offeror.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · When does acceptance take effect?

questions.q: A neighbour paints your fence as a favour; later you promise $500 for it. Can they enforce the promise?
choices: Yes, the work had real value to you
No, it's past consideration
Yes, if the promise was in writing
Only if the amount is reasonable
questions.explain: Consideration must be given in exchange for the promise. Something already done is past consideration.

questions.q: Will a court set aside a land sale because the price was only $1?
choices: Yes, the price must be fair market value
Not usually; courts don't review adequacy
Yes, unless a lawyer approved the deal
Only if the buyer is a related person
questions.explain: Courts don't weigh adequacy, absent fraud, duress or similar problems.

questions.q: What did Pooni v. Storsley lead to on the standard contract form?
choices: The seal was removed from the standard form
Initial boxes so parties knowingly adopt a seal
A new requirement for a lawyer's sign-off
A minimum deposit amount for every contract
questions.explain: A seal replaces consideration only if knowingly applied, so the form now has initial boxes beside the seal.

questions.q: What's the safest way to make a binding amendment to a contract of purchase and sale?
choices: Get a verbal agreement from both of the parties
In writing, with nominal consideration or a seal
Email the other party's licensee about the change
Have only the buyer sign the amendment form
questions.explain: Rosas v. Toca suggests fresh consideration may not be needed, but writing plus $1 or a seal is safest.

questions.q: In the Tapestry case, why did the licensee get 7% instead of 10% commission?
choices: The client negotiated it down after the closing
The 10% wasn't initialled, so a fair rate applied
BCFSA caps every commission at 7% of the price
The brokerage chose to waive the remaining 3%
questions.explain: No agreed rate was proven, so the court awarded a reasonable amount (quantum meruit): 7%.

questions.q: Two strangers sign a commercial lease. What does the law presume about legal intention?
choices: No intention, unless proven
An intention to be legally bound
Nothing either way
Intention only if a lawyer is involved
questions.explain: Commercial deals between strangers are presumed intended to be binding; family arrangements are presumed not.

questions.q: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy a condo. Which is correct?
choices: The seller can enforce it against the minor
The minor can enforce it against the seller
It's automatically void for both sides
It becomes binding at age 18
questions.explain: Under the Infants Act, contracts are unenforceable against minors (under 19) but enforceable by them.

questions.q: Which makes a contract signed as a minor enforceable against them?
choices: Turning 18 before completion
Affirming it after turning 19
Signing it in front of a witness
A parent's verbal approval
questions.explain: Exceptions: a statute says so, affirmed after 19, performed within a year, or not repudiated within a year of turning 19.

questions.q: Under the Adult Guardianship Act s.60.2, when does a transfer by a mentally incapable person stand?
choices: Only if the person's doctor approved the sale beforehand
If a fair price was paid, or incapacity wasn't knowable
Never; all such transfers are automatically void
Only if the buyer is a member of the seller's family
questions.explain: A transfer survives if the buyer paid full and fair value, or had no reasonable way to know of the incapacity.

questions.q: How long can a non-enduring power of attorney be used for land under the Land Title Act s.56?
choices: 1 year
3 years
5 years
Indefinitely
questions.explain: Generally 3 years, unless it's an enduring power of attorney.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Powers of attorney and related documents

questions.q: What's special about an enduring power of attorney?
choices: It ends when the donor loses mental capacity
It continues after the donor loses capacity
It only covers personal health care decisions
It can only be granted by a court order
questions.explain: An enduring POA survives incapacity and isn't subject to the 3-year land limit.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Powers of attorney and related documents

questions.q: Can a representation agreement made after September 1, 2011 be used to sell real estate?
choices: Yes, always
No
Only with a court order
Only for strata lots
questions.explain: Representation agreements made after that date can't authorize real estate sales. Use a POA or committee.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Powers of attorney and related documents

questions.q: Which does NOT end an ordinary power of attorney?
choices: The donor's death
Using it to pay bills
The donor's bankruptcy
The donor's incapacity
questions.explain: Death, bankruptcy and incapacity end an ordinary POA (not an enduring one). Paying bills is just using it.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Powers of attorney and related documents

questions.q: What does non est factum mean?
choices: "Let the buyer beware"
"It is not my deed"
"As much as he deserved"
"Things speak for themselves"
questions.explain: A defence for someone who signed without knowing the document's fundamental nature, without carelessness.

questions.q: An executor wants to list a deceased owner's house before probate is granted. What's best?
choices: List it, and complete without probate
List it subject to probate being granted
Wait until a joint tenant is found
Have the heirs sign the contract instead
questions.explain: The executor can list subject to probate (often 3–6 months). An administrator has no authority before Letters of Administration.

questions.q: In Shafazand, why did the court refuse the claim over the illegal suite?
choices: The buyer waited too long to sue the seller
Courts may refuse relief on an illegal contract
The suite was disclosed in the PDS
Damages for suites are capped by statute
questions.explain: Hiding an illegal suite tainted the deal; the court denied the $42K claim.

questions.q: What remedy does an innocent misrepresentation give, generally?
choices: Damages and rescission at any time
Rescission, but only before completion
Damages only, but no rescission
No remedy at all, ever
questions.explain: Innocent misrepresentation: rescission before completion, no damages. Fraud: rescission any time plus damages.

questions.q: Who does an entire agreement clause NOT protect?
choices: A seller who made an innocent misstatement
A licensee who made the misrepresentation
Either party, as to pre-contract talk
A seller as to innocent statements in ads
questions.explain: It never protects licensees, and never protects anyone against fraud.

questions.q: A crack in a basement wall is visible on a reasonable inspection. What is it?
choices: A latent defect
A patent defect
A stigma
A material latent defect
questions.explain: Patent defects are discoverable by reasonable inspection, so they're generally the buyer's problem.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Defects: caveat emptor and its limits

questions.q: Under common law, when must a seller disclose a latent defect?
choices: Always, whether or not they know about it
When known and dangerous, or making it uninhabitable
Only if the buyer asks them about it directly, in writing
Never; caveat emptor applies to every kind of defect
questions.explain: Known latent defects that are dangerous or make the property uninhabitable must be disclosed.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Defects: caveat emptor and its limits

questions.q: In Gibb v. Sprague, which defect made the seller liable?
choices: Ants the seller didn't know about
Mould the seller knew of and hid
Patent electrical problems
Old windows needing paint
questions.explain: Known, concealed mould: liable. Unknown ants and patent electrical issues: not.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Defects: caveat emptor and its limits

questions.q: Under Rules s.59, which is a material latent defect the seller's licensee must disclose?
choices: A neighbour's noisy dog
Work done without the required permits
A suicide in the home 10 years ago
An older but working furnace
questions.explain: Material latent defects include work without permits, local government notices, danger, unfitness and great expense to fix.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · The licensee's wider duty: Rules s.59

questions.q: Your seller client tells you not to disclose a material latent defect. What must you do?
choices: Follow the instruction; it's lawful
Stop acting for that client
Disclose it only if the buyer asks
Put it in the contract's fine print
questions.explain: You can't follow that instruction; you must stop acting for the seller.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · The licensee's wider duty: Rules s.59

questions.q: At what radon level does BCFSA treat it as a material latent defect?
choices: Above 100 Bq/m³
Above 200 Bq/m³
Above 400 Bq/m³
Any detectable radon
questions.explain: Radon above 200 Bq/m³ (Health Canada's guideline) is treated as a material latent defect.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · The licensee's wider duty: Rules s.59

questions.q: A buyer asks whether anyone died in the home. What should you do?
choices: Lie to protect your seller client
Tell the truth or decline to answer
Tell them it's illegal to ask that
Say nothing and change the subject
questions.explain: Stigmas aren't defects, so there's no duty to volunteer them; but if asked, never lie. Answer truthfully or decline.

questions.q: Both parties sign a deal for a cabin that, unknown to them, burned down the day before. What's the result?
choices: Voidable at the buyer's option
Void for common mistake
Valid; the buyer bears the risk
Frustrated, so the deposit is kept
questions.explain: Common mistake about the existence of the subject matter makes the contract void.

questions.q: What separates common mistake from frustration?
choices: Common mistake applies only to contracts for land
Mistake exists before signing; frustration comes after
Frustration requires fault by one of the parties
They're simply two names for the same doctrine
questions.explain: Common mistake: before the contract. Frustration: an outside event after the contract.

questions.q: An elderly client signs after their caregiver dominates the decision. What's the likely ground?
choices: Duress
Undue influence
Frustration
Common mistake
questions.explain: A dominant relationship influencing the weaker party is undue influence, which makes the contract voidable.
questions.ref: Lesson 7 · Duress, undue influence and unconscionability

questions.q: Who can waive a condition precedent under LEA s.54?
choices: Either party, at any time before completion
The sole beneficiary, before the deadline
Only the seller, since it's their property
Only a court, on application by a party
questions.explain: Only the party for whose sole benefit it exists can waive it, and only before the deadline.

questions.q: What wording helps make a subject waivable by one party?
choices: "Subject to approval"
"For the sole benefit of the Buyer"
"Time is of the essence in this contract"
"This is the entire agreement"
questions.explain: Saying it's for the sole benefit of one party lets that party waive it.

questions.q: In Capital Quality Homes, what was the effect of rezoning after the contract?
choices: The buyer was required to complete anyway
It was frustrated and the deposit returned
The seller had to pay the buyer damages
It was rescinded for common mistake
questions.explain: Rezoning made performance fundamentally different, so the contract was frustrated.

questions.q: What can the innocent party do after a breach of warranty?
choices: End the contract and claim damages
Claim damages but still perform
Get specific performance only
Nothing, as warranties are minor
questions.explain: A warranty is a minor term: damages only, and the contract continues.

questions.q: In Gill v. Bal, the buyer paid at 5:36 p.m. on a 4 p.m. deadline. What happened?
choices: The court gave the buyer a 24-hour grace period
The buyer was in breach and the contract ended
The seller had to accept the late payment
The deadline was invalid for vagueness
questions.explain: Time was of the essence; missing it was a fundamental breach.

questions.q: What does Rules s.48 prohibit?
choices: Presenting more than one offer at a time
Inducing a party to break a contract
Writing subjects into an offer
Holding deposits in trust
questions.explain: Licensees must never induce a party to breach a contract, e.g. to switch to a better deal.

questions.q: Which is required for a statutory assignment under LEA s.36?
choices: The original promisor's consent
Written notice to the promisor
Registration of the assignment at the LTO
A seal on the assignment document
questions.explain: Statutory assignment: in writing, absolute and unconditional, with written notice to the promisor.

questions.q: Under the standard assignment terms in Regulation s.8.2, who gets any assignment profit?
choices: The buyer who assigns
The seller
The brokerage
The assignee
questions.explain: No assignment without the seller's written consent, and the seller gets any profit.

questions.q: Which remedy is equitable and discretionary?
choices: Damages
Specific performance
Liquidated damages
Interest on deposits
questions.explain: Damages are a common law right; specific performance and injunctions are equitable and discretionary.

questions.q: When will a court treat a liquidated damages clause as a penalty?
choices: When it's a genuine pre-estimate of loss
When it isn't a genuine pre-estimate of loss
Whenever the amount exceeds 10%
Only in residential contracts
questions.explain: A genuine pre-estimate is enforced; otherwise it's an unenforceable penalty.

questions.q: What principle comes from Hadley v. Baxendale?
choices: The duty to act in good faith
Damages for natural or foreseeable losses only
Courts don't review adequacy of consideration
Contracts for land must be in writing
questions.explain: Recoverable damages are those arising naturally or reasonably foreseeable at contracting.

questions.q: After a breach, what must the innocent party do about their losses?
choices: Nothing; the wrongdoer pays for everything
Take reasonable steps to mitigate them
Wait for the court to tell them what to do
Report them to BCFSA before doing anything
questions.explain: The innocent party must mitigate; they can't recover losses they could reasonably have avoided.
